cards.t: The coronary arteries and their branches
q: what are the coronary arteries
what are the branches of the left main coronary artery
which coronary artery supplies the right side
cards.x:
The heart muscle is fed by two coronary arteries, and every heart disease that follows is a problem of supply through them. The left main coronary artery divides into two branches. One is the left anterior descending artery, also called the anterior interventricular branch because it runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus, a groove on the heart's surface. The other is the circumflex branch. The right coronary artery runs in the coronary sulcus. It gives off the marginal branch and the posterior interventricular branch.

Reduced to four labels: right coronary artery, left main, left anterior descending and left circumflex. Worth remembering that nearly every infarct (area of dead heart muscle) is in the wall of the left ventricle. The left anterior descending territory is the most common.

cards.t: What sets the heart's oxygen demand
q: what determines the heart's oxygen demand
what are the four determinants of cardiac workload
what increases myocardial oxygen demand
cards.x:
Four things set how hard the heart works and so how much oxygen it needs: heart rate, preload, afterload and contractility. An increase in any one of them increases the demand for oxygen.

Preload is how much the muscle fibers are stretched by filling before they contract. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle has to push against. Contractility is how forcefully the muscle squeezes. This is the demand half of every ischemia question. Ischemia (too little oxygen for the muscle's needs) appears when the supply cannot keep up with this demand.

q: what is the Frank-Starling law
why does a fuller ventricle pump harder
why does dilation only help so far
cards.x:
The Frank-Starling law says that the more the ventricle fills during diastole (the relaxing and filling phase), the more blood it ejects in the systole (the squeeze) that follows. The reason sits in the muscle fibers. The force a single fiber generates is proportional to its starting sarcomere length (how stretched its contractile units are, which is the preload). That stretch is set by how full the ventricle is at the end of diastole.

So a fuller heart pumps harder, but the law describes the benefit of stretch only up to a point. A ventricle that dilates keeps stretching its fibers, which is why dilation helps only so far.

q: what is the difference between LDL and VLDL
which lipoprotein is protective
how do lipoproteins change heart disease risk
cards.x:
Plaques are made of lipid (fat), and lipid travels in the blood bound to proteins, so which lipoprotein is carrying it changes the risk.

- LDL (low-density lipoprotein) carries cholesterol and carries the highest risk.
- VLDL (very low density lipoprotein) is high in triglycerides rather than cholesterol, and it also increases risk.
- HDL (high-density lipoprotein) decreases risk: it carries cholesterol back to the liver, clearing it away from plaque.

Quick way to tell the first two apart: both raise risk, so the difference is simply what each one is carrying, cholesterol for LDL and triglycerides for VLDL.

q: what is familial hypercholesterolemia
what is the defect in familial hypercholesterolemia
what causes genetic hyperlipidemia
cards.x:
Familial hypercholesterolemia is a common single-gene form of genetic hyperlipidemia (too much fat in the blood). It is classically taught as the most common form. The defect is in the low-density lipoprotein receptor on liver cells. That receptor is how the liver pulls cholesterol-carrying particles out of the blood. Without working receptors, the liver cannot remove cholesterol from the bloodstream and it builds up.

Genetic hyperlipidemia also has an acquired counterpart, meaning the version you pick up rather than inherit: a high-fat diet.

cards.t: The four mechanisms behind heart disease
q: what are the mechanisms of heart disease
how do you sort heart diseases by what goes wrong
what is the difference between pressure work and volume work
cards.x:
Common heart diseases reduce to one of four mechanisms, sorted by which structure is failing.

- Coronary arteries: oxygen supply falls below demand. This covers stable, variant and unstable angina and myocardial infarction.
- Valves: extra pressure work (stenosis, forcing blood through a smaller opening) or extra volume work (regurgitation, blood leaking back and needing to be pumped again). This covers mitral and aortic stenosis and regurgitation, and prolapse.
- Myocardium (the heart muscle): inflammation, dilation, hypertrophy or stiffening of the muscle itself. This covers myocarditis and dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
- Pericardium (the sac around the heart): external compression or encasement that limits filling. This covers effusion and tamponade, and constrictive pericarditis.

q: what is homocysteine
how does homocysteine damage blood vessels
cards.x:
Homocysteine is an intermediary amino acid, formed along the way when the body converts methionine to cysteine. It has mainly atherogenic properties (it promotes atherosclerosis) and prothrombotic ones (it promotes clotting).

The vascular injury it causes includes:
- Thickening of the inner layer.
- Disruption of the elastic lamina (the elastic layer in the vessel wall).
- Smooth muscle hypertrophy.
- Large platelet accumulation, and a platelet-enriched thrombus that can block the vessel.

q: what molecules recruit monocytes in atherosclerosis
what degrades the fibrous cap of a plaque
how does a plaque go from early lesion to vulnerable plaque
cards.x:
The molecular story of a plaque runs in three stages.

First, initiation. Atherogenic factors (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, diabetes, hypertension, smoking) cause endothelial dysfunction. Signals such as monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (a chemical that attracts monocytes) and vascular cell adhesion molecule (which lets monocytes stick to the lining) recruit monocytes. Vascular smooth muscle cells also activate.

Second, the early lesion. Foam cells form the fatty streak. Growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor drive smooth muscle cells to migrate and multiply.

Third, the vulnerable plaque. It has a thin fibrous cap (the smooth muscle cells in it are dying by apoptosis, programmed cell death), a lipid core full of foam cells, and intense inflammation at the shoulder. Collagenases, elastases and stromelysins are enzymes that chew up the wall's structural proteins. They degrade the cap until it ruptures.

cards.t: Coronary heart disease: definition and causes
q: what is coronary heart disease
what causes coronary heart disease
what are the uncommon causes of coronary heart disease
cards.x:
Coronary heart disease, also called ischemic heart disease or coronary artery disease, is insufficient delivery of oxygenated blood to the heart muscle because the coronary arteries are atherosclerotic. About 50% of the people who die of cardiovascular disease die of it. When the heart's demand for oxygen exceeds the supply, the muscle becomes ischemic. That causes abnormal heart function and abnormal rhythms and, if prolonged, irreversible damage.

The causes:
- Atherosclerosis, behind almost all of it. The lumen (the open channel) narrows progressively, which predisposes to thrombosis, coronary vasospasm and endothelial dysfunction.
- Abnormal microcirculation: the small cardiac vessels are regulated abnormally by their endothelial cells.
- Uncommon: decreased oxygen content of the blood (the arteries are open but the blood carries too little).
- Uncommon: poor perfusion from hypotension or hypovolemia (too little pressure to drive flow).

cards.t: Risk factors for coronary heart disease
k: risk factors for ischemic heart disease
q: what are the risk factors for coronary heart disease
what is the most important risk factor for atherosclerosis
cards.x:
Risk factors for coronary heart disease include age, family history, abnormal lipids, cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus and obesity. Male sex, homocysteine and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (a blood marker of inflammation) are also on the list.

Two extra points. Family history is described as the most important risk factor for atherosclerosis. C-reactive protein is now used in cardiovascular risk stratification, meaning sorting people by how likely they are to have a cardiovascular event.

cards.t: How a coronary atherosclerotic plaque forms
q: how does atherosclerosis start
what are the steps in plaque formation
how do foam cells form
when does a plaque start to limit blood flow
cards.x:
A plaque is the wall's response to injury, built in a sequence.

Injury to the endothelial cells starts it (from chronic hemodynamic wall stress, toxins, inflammation or hyperlipidemia). The injured endothelium becomes more permeable and leukocytes (white cells) are recruited. Low-density lipoprotein leaks through into the wall, where cells and macrophages oxidize it, and the oxidized lipid damages the wall and its smooth muscle cells. More macrophages arrive and keep engulfing lipid; the lipid-filled ones become foam cells. Both kinds of macrophage release inflammatory mediators and growth factor, which attract more leukocytes and stimulate smooth muscle to multiply. Excess lipid and debris pool inside the wall as the lipid core.

Later, collagen and fibrin form a cap, which makes the plaque more stable. Plaques grow over years until they begin to occlude the lumen, and blood flow is compromised at 75% occlusion, so it takes a great deal of narrowing before flow suffers.

q: what makes a plaque vulnerable
what is the difference between a stable and a vulnerable plaque
which plaques rupture
cards.x:
A vulnerable plaque is one that is likely to erode or rupture. What matters is its makeup, not only how narrow it makes the artery. It has:
- A large lipid (necrotic) core under a thin fibrous cap.
- Lots of macrophages.
- Increased matrix metalloproteinases (enzymes that break down the wall's structural proteins).
- Few smooth muscle cells.
- Low-grade stenosis (only mild narrowing).

That last feature is the surprising one: the plaque that ruptures need not be the one narrowing the artery most.

A stable plaque instead has a thick fibrous cap, a small lipid core and plenty of smooth muscle cells. A neat way to remember the roles: smooth muscle cells build the cap and macrophages digest it.

cards.t: Why plaques rupture and what happens next
q: what causes a plaque to rupture
what happens when a plaque ruptures
how does shear force affect a plaque
cards.x:
Plaque rupture risk depends on the plaque's composition and the mechanical stresses on it. A vulnerable plaque (large necrotic core, thin fibrous cap) can be broken by a triggering event of enough magnitude and duration. One example is the shear force of blood flowing at high velocity through a severe stenosis. The diseased wall may also be rich in vasa vasorum capillaries. Their thin walls hemorrhage, depositing blood products and building pressure inside the plaque.

Factors that make a plaque vulnerable to erosion or rupture include intra-plaque inflammation, a large core with a thin cap, superficial platelet aggregation and severe stenosis. Still, the plaque that ruptures need not be the one narrowing the artery most. When a plaque ruptures, it exposes subendothelial proteins. These start platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. The consequence is thrombosis, and emboli carried downstream to block smaller vessels.

q: what is cardiac ischemia
what causes cardiac ischemia
why is a slow blockage tolerated better than a sudden one
cards.x:
Ischemia starts when oxygen supply is insufficient for the demand of the cardiac cells. With less oxygen, less adenosine triphosphate (ATP, the cell's energy currency) is formed. Every cause falls on one side of a balance.

- Supply falls with large atherosclerotic plaques, acute platelet aggregation then thrombosis, vasospasm, abnormal microcirculation and poor perfusion pressures.
- Demand rises with heart rate, preload, afterload and contractility.

Myocardial oxygen consumption and blood flow correspond nearly linearly. When plaque builds slowly over years, the heart develops collateral circulation (backup vessels) to keep the muscle perfused. That is one reason a slow occlusion can be tolerated and a sudden one cannot. Abrupt occlusion of a previously healthy vessel can do more damage than a severe chronic stenosis.

q: how are coronary syndromes classified
what is the dividing line between chronic and acute coronary syndromes
cards.x:
Coronary syndromes are classified by the severity and onset of cardiac symptoms. The chronic ones are stable angina and ischemic cardiomyopathy; the acute ones are unstable angina and myocardial infarction.

The dividing line is mechanism. The chronic syndromes come from a fixed narrowing that fails only when demand rises. The acute ones come from plaque rupture with acute thrombosis.

cards.t: Angina pectoris: stable, Prinzmetal and unstable
q: what is angina
what is the difference between stable, variant and unstable angina
what causes Prinzmetal angina
cards.x:
Angina is intermittent cardiac ischemia that is not enough to kill cardiac cells. It usually happens when the heart's oxygen demand rises (Prinzmetal angina, below, is the exception). It may cause insufficient pumping, leading to pulmonary congestion.

- Stable (typical) angina is the most common. Stenotic atherosclerotic vessels reduce flow to a critical level. So perfusion is adequate at rest but inadequate under increased cardiac workload.
- Prinzmetal (variant) angina: vasospasm (the artery suddenly tightening) is the probable mechanism, though its cause is unknown. It is unpredictable and typically happens at rest rather than with exertion.
- Unstable (crescendo) angina may progress to acute ischemia, which is why it is classed with the acute coronary syndromes.

q: what is the difference between angina and a myocardial infarction
what is acute coronary syndrome
why are unstable angina and MI grouped together
cards.x:
The difference between angina and myocardial infarction (heart attack) is whether heart muscle cells die. Angina is intermittent ischemia that is insufficient to kill cardiac cells. Myocardial infarction results from prolonged or total disruption of blood flow. That causes cell death by necrosis or apoptosis.

Unstable angina and myocardial infarction are grouped together as acute coronary syndrome because they are hard to distinguish clinically. In both, the pain lasts longer than typical angina, and plaque rupture with acute thrombosis is thought to occur.

q: what happens in a myocardial infarction
how does plaque rupture cause a heart attack
what decides how much damage an occlusion does
cards.x:
A myocardial infarction starts with thrombosis on top of an ulcerated or cracked atherosclerotic plaque. Platelets adhere to the ruptured plaque and form a platelet plug, the clotting cascade is activated, and a growing thrombus occludes the vessel.

What the occlusion does depends on collateral circulation, the heart's workload and the length of time. A typical infarct has several zones of cells in various stages of necrosis.

cards.t: What happens to the muscle after total occlusion
q: how long until heart muscle dies after a blockage
how does an infarct change over time
when does an infarct become a scar
cards.x:
When a coronary artery is completely occluded, the injury follows a pattern. Immediately, the cell's energy store, adenosine triphosphate (ATP), is depleted. After a few minutes, the muscle can no longer contract. After 30 minutes, cell necrosis becomes irreversible.

The infarcted area then changes in appearance. For the first several hours it is hard to see with the naked eye (the classic teaching puts the first visible change at about 6 hours). At 18 to 24 hours it turns paler. Then it becomes yellowish and soft with a border of red vascular connective tissue. At 1 to 2 weeks the necrotic tissue is taken away, and by 6 weeks a tough fibrous scar has formed. The scar does not contract.

k: which artery is most often responsible for MI
q: which coronary artery is most often responsible for infarcts
where do myocardial infarcts happen
cards.x:
Nearly all myocardial infarcts are in the walls of the left ventricle. By the artery responsible:

- Left anterior descending: 40 to 50%, the most common.
- Right coronary: 30 to 40%.
- Left circumflex: 15 to 20%.

So almost every infarct lands in the left ventricle's wall. The left anterior descending is the artery most often responsible, followed by the right coronary and then the left circumflex.

q: what is the difference between stenosis and regurgitation
what damages heart valves
why do valve problems cause heart failure
cards.x:
Heart valves are damaged by inflammation with scarring (mitral or aortic), calcification (mitral or aortic), or congenital defects (present from birth, in any valve). The altered hemodynamics (how blood flows and what pressures it creates) raise cardiac workload, and heart failure may result.

- Stenosis is failure of the valve to open completely. It means pressure work: blood is forced through a smaller opening, and a pressure gradient (a pressure difference) forms across the valve. It begins to affect hemodynamics at 50% closure and progresses slowly, so the heart compensates by growing thicker muscle cells (hypertrophy). Primary causes: post-inflammatory scarring from rheumatic fever, and aging valvular calcification.
- Regurgitation is inability of the valve to close completely. It means volume work: blood flows back across the valve and must be pumped again. Acute regurgitation comes from infection or papillary muscle rupture. Important causes include rheumatic heart disease and infective endocarditis, as well as degenerative valve changes and aortic root dilation.

q: what happens in mitral stenosis
why does mitral stenosis cause atrial fibrillation
why does mitral stenosis cause pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
In mitral stenosis the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle cannot open fully, so during diastole there is an abnormal gradient (a pressure difference): atrial pressure stays higher than ventricular pressure, and the gradient grows as the stenosis worsens.

The problem sits upstream of the ventricle. The left atrium becomes congested and its pressure rises, pulmonary pressures rise, and the left ventricular stroke volume decreases; the ventricle is not diseased, it is simply not being filled. Atrial enlargement and hypertrophy lead to pulmonary hypertension and then right-sided hypertrophy and failure. With progression, the increased atrial volume leads to atrial fibrillation, and the enlarged, fibrillating atrium is prone to atrial clots.

q: what happens in mitral regurgitation
why does high afterload worsen mitral regurgitation
cards.x:
In mitral regurgitation blood leaks backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole. A high afterload increases the amount regurgitated: the blood takes the path of least resistance, so the harder it is to eject forward, the more goes backward.

The left atrial volume and pressure rise. The left ventricle has to pump a greater volume to keep an effective stroke volume, so both the atrium and the ventricle dilate and hypertrophy. If it is severe, left-sided heart failure follows. Acute regurgitation comes from infection or papillary muscle rupture.

q: what is mitral valve prolapse
does mitral valve prolapse cause symptoms
cards.x:
Mitral valve prolapse is ballooning of the mitral valve back into the left atrium during systole. It usually causes no symptoms. In a few cases the ballooning is enough to cause some mitral regurgitation, meaning a little blood leaks backward into the atrium with each squeeze.

Do not confuse it with stenosis: prolapse is a valve that bulges back too far while the ventricle squeezes, whereas stenosis is a valve that cannot open fully. Like mitral regurgitation, it is a problem of systole.

q: what causes aortic stenosis
why does aortic stenosis cause angina
what happens to the left ventricle in aortic stenosis
cards.x:
In aortic stenosis the aortic valve cannot open fully in systole. So there is an obstruction to outflow and a gradient between the left ventricle and the aorta. It is most commonly caused by age-related calcification, which is common with a bicuspid aortic valve. Rheumatic disease is an uncommon cause, and it usually shows up years after the original rheumatic fever.

The ventricle has to generate high systolic pressures, and it slowly hypertrophies. Hypertrophy plus high pressure raise oxygen demand beyond what supply can meet. So they predispose to ischemia and angina, and angina can arise even with entirely normal coronary arteries. It may also lead to left heart failure.

q: what happens in aortic regurgitation
what causes aortic regurgitation
cards.x:
In aortic regurgitation an incompetent valve leaks blood from the aorta back into the left ventricle during diastole. The causes are similar to those of mitral regurgitation, and dilation of the aortic root (from aging or connective tissue disease) is a common one.

The left ventricle hypertrophies and dilates, and the aortic diastolic pressure falls because blood leaks back into the ventricle. The high workload can lead to left-sided heart failure.

cards.t: Systole or diastole: placing each valve problem
q: how do I remember which valve problems happen in diastole
how do I work out the consequence of a valve lesion
cards.x:
Timing is the whole trick. Mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation are problems in diastole. Mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse and aortic stenosis are problems in systole.

To work out the consequence of any valve lesion, ask which chamber is filling or emptying across the bad valve. For example, in mitral stenosis the ventricle is not diseased, it is simply not being filled, so the trouble lies upstream in the atrium.

q: what is rheumatic heart disease
how does rheumatic fever damage the heart
is rheumatic heart damage caused by the bacteria itself
cards.x:
Rheumatic heart disease is an uncommon but serious consequence of rheumatic fever, the acute inflammatory disease that follows infection with group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus. The damage is an immune attack caused by cross-reactivity, not by the bacteria themselves. There is a genetic predisposition seen in certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types.

The inflammation involves all layers of the heart (carditis). In the endocardium (the heart's inner lining) it causes valvular swelling, erosions, and platelet aggregation and fibrin on the leaflets. With progression, the valve structures scar and shorten.

q: what is infective endocarditis
what is a vegetation on a heart valve
what organisms cause endocarditis
cards.x:
Infective endocarditis is invasion and colonization of the endocardial structures by pathogens (germs), causing inflammation. Invasion of the bloodstream is a prerequisite.

Vegetations form: clumps of microbes enmeshed in fibrin deposits. As they grow large they interfere with valve function and predispose to emboli (pieces that break off and travel). The most common culprits are Streptococcus strains and Staphylococcus aureus.

q: what is subacute endocarditis
why does Staphylococcus aureus cause acute endocarditis
which endocarditis needs a damaged valve
cards.x:
Subacute infective endocarditis has an insidious (slow, sneaky) onset in people with a preexisting valve pathology. The germs involved are less virulent, typically Streptococcus, and are not virulent enough to attack a healthy endocardium, so the damaged valve is what lets them in.

Staphylococcus aureus belongs on the other side. It is highly virulent: it is the classic cause of acute endocarditis and can attack a normal valve. The general rule is that the less virulent the germ, the more it depends on an already-damaged valve.

q: what is myocarditis
what causes myocarditis
what does the heart look like in myocarditis
cards.x:
Myocarditis is inflammation, leukocyte infiltration and necrosis of the myocardium. Causes include microbes (most often viruses, classically Coxsackievirus), immune-related disease and physical agents.

The picture is left ventricular dysfunction, sometimes with dilation of the chambers. There are patchy or diffuse necrotic lesions, and inflamed, edematous muscle with leukocyte infiltrates. The endocardial structures are usually normal.

q: what are the types of cardiomyopathy
what is the difference between dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy
what causes dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle. Some have known causes; those of unknown cause are grouped by their major pathophysiological feature.

- Dilated (also called congested): dilation of one or both ventricles, leading to cardiac failure with dilation. Associated factors are alcohol, genetics, pregnancy and a post-viral state.
- Hypertrophic: a thickened, hyperkinetic ventricular muscle mass, with symptoms from ventricular outflow obstruction and impaired diastolic filling.
- Restrictive: a stiff, fibrotic, rigid, noncompliant ventricle, most are related to a specific condition such as amyloidosis. Diastolic filling is restricted, so stroke volume is low and heart failure follows.

Two of the three fail in filling (hypertrophic and restrictive) and one fails in emptying (dilated).

q: what is cardiac tamponade
what causes pericardial effusion
what kinds of fluid can collect around the heart
cards.x:
Cardiac tamponade is what happens when pericardial fluid, especially if it collects quickly, compresses the heart chambers from outside so that filling is impaired; it is life-threatening. The muscle and valves may be entirely normal while output collapses.

The fluid comes from pericardial disease, which is rarely primary and usually secondary to another cause. Whatever the cause, fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac (the sac around the heart), and when the cause is inflammatory the pericardial structures can become painfully inflamed. The type of fluid points to the cause:

- Serous (a transudate, a thin watery fluid): secondary to heart failure or hypoproteinemia.
- Serosanguinous (serous fluid plus blood): after blunt chest trauma, heart surgery or cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
- Chylous (lymph): from obstruction to lymph drainage.
- Blood (hemopericardium): from penetrating cardiac trauma.

An effusion is simply a collection of fluid; it is often a non-inflammatory, watery fluid, but it can also be an inflammatory exudate when infection or inflammation is the cause.

q: what is constrictive pericarditis
what causes acute pericarditis
what is adhesive mediastinopericarditis
cards.x:
Acute pericarditis is mostly idiopathic (no cause found), and most of those cases are viral; the inflammation damages the pericardium. Healing of an acute form can leave chronic dysfunction (the healed, chronic forms), and there are two principal types.

- Adhesive mediastinopericarditis follows suppurative (pus-forming) or caseous pericarditis, or surgery. The sac is destroyed and the heart adheres to the surrounding mediastinal structures, so every beat pulls against them and workload rises.
- Constrictive pericarditis has many causes that are unknown, and can share the adhesive form's causes. The sac becomes dense, nonelastic, fibrous and scarred and encases the heart like a stiff cage, which impairs diastolic filling.

cards.t: Tamponade versus constrictive pericarditis versus restrictive cardiomyopathy
q: what is the difference between tamponade, constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy
what stops the heart from filling
cards.x:
These three problems all stop the heart from filling properly, but the anatomy is different in each.

- Cardiac tamponade: fluid around the heart, compressing the chambers from outside.
- Constrictive pericarditis: a scarred, fibrous cage around the heart.
- Restrictive cardiomyopathy: a stiff, noncompliant muscle within the heart.

The effect on filling is the same, with diastolic filling restricted. What differs is where the problem sits: in the sac's fluid, in the sac's wall, or in the muscle itself.

cards.t: The three layers of a blood vessel wall
q: what are the three layers of a blood vessel
what is the media of an artery made of
what are the vasa vasorum
cards.x:
Arteries and veins both have three layers, though they are more clearly separated in the thicker arterial wall.

- Intima: a single layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane, with a thin underlying layer of extracellular matrix.
- Media: in elastic arteries such as the aorta, lamellar units of elastin fibers and smooth muscle cells arranged like tree rings, which expand during systole and recoil during diastole.
- Adventitia: loose connective tissue for support. It can carry nerve fibers, and in large vessels it holds their own small arterioles (the vasa vasorum), which perfuse the adventitia and part of the media.

The amount of smooth muscle and matrix in the media varies with the hemodynamic demand where the vessel sits. Capillaries are the exception: they have no media.

q: what are capillaries like
what are the types of capillaries
why is exchange easy across capillaries
which tissues have the most capillaries
cards.x:
A capillary is about the diameter of a red blood cell or slightly smaller. Red cells must deform to pass, which brings their membranes into close contact with the endothelium. Its lumen is lined with endothelium and it has no media; pericytes wrap around it. Capillaries have a large total cross-sectional area and a low flow rate. Thin walls plus slow flow make exchange easy. Tissues with high metabolic rates, the myocardium and brain, have the highest capillary density.

Three types:
- Continuous: the least permeable, as in the blood-brain barrier.
- Fenestrated: has windows (kidney glomeruli, small intestine).
- Sinusoidal: gaps, large fenestrations and a discontinuous basement membrane (liver, bone marrow, spleen, endocrine glands).

cards.t: The hepatic portal system and first pass
q: what is the hepatic portal system
why do drugs get metabolized on first pass
where do veins from the intestines go
cards.x:
The hepatic portal system is the set of veins that carries blood from the stomach and intestines into the liver. That arrangement means nutrients absorbed from the gut are processed by the liver, and drugs are metabolized there on first pass, meaning the liver gets to them first.

So the liver gets the first look at what the gut has absorbed.

cards.t: How vessel structure changes from artery to vein
q: what is the difference between an elastic and a muscular artery
how does the structure of blood vessels change
what is the wall of an arteriole like
cards.x:
Following the blood from the heart and back, the vessels change structure to suit their job.

- Elastic artery (the aorta): elastin fibers between smooth muscle, which let the wall expand in systole and recoil in diastole.
- Muscular artery: densely packed concentric smooth muscle.
- Arteriole: the point of blood pressure control.
- Capillary: only endothelium and pericytes, built for gas and nutrient exchange.
- Then the post-capillary venule, medium vein and large vein.

The amount of smooth muscle and matrix in the wall varies with the hemodynamic demand where the vessel sits.

cards.t: What each type of blood vessel does
q: what do arterioles do
what is the function of veins
why are arterioles called the points of resistance
how much blood do veins hold
cards.x:
Overall, the vascular system transports nutrients to the tissues, carries waste away and moves hormones from one part of the body to another. It also keeps tissue fluids in balance for the cells' function. Each segment has its own job.

- Arteries: high pressure, strong walls, high-velocity flow.
- Arterioles: the control conduits that release blood into the capillaries and the principal points of resistance to flow ("small but mighty").
- Capillaries: exchange of fluid, nutrients, electrolytes, hormones and wastes between blood and tissue.
- Venules: collect blood from capillaries and join into larger veins.
- Veins: return blood to the heart and act as the major reservoir of extra blood, with low pressure and thin walls.

Veins hold about 66% of the total blood volume, so maintaining that volume is a large part of maintaining blood pressure.

k: why the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood
q: why does the pulmonary artery carry deoxygenated blood
what is the difference between pulmonary and systemic circulation
cards.x:
There are two loops. The pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs. The systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart to the tissues, and returns deoxygenated blood to the right side.

The naming rule that settles the confusion: an artery carries blood away from the heart and a vein carries it toward the heart, whatever the oxygen content. That is why the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

cards.t: What endothelial and smooth muscle cells do
q: what do endothelial cells do
why doesn't blood clot inside healthy vessels
what do vascular smooth muscle cells do
cards.x:
Endothelial cells are specialized simple squamous epithelium that lines the lumen. They maintain vessel homeostasis. They also provide a nonthrombogenic surface that keeps blood fluid. That is an active property, so endothelial injury lets platelets adhere and a thrombus begin. They modulate the tone of the smooth muscle in the media, and so vascular resistance. They also metabolize hormones such as angiotensin, regulate inflammation, and affect the growth of other cells, particularly smooth muscle.

Smooth muscle cells are the predominant cell of the media. They are responsible for vasoconstriction and vasodilation and for normal vascular repair. They play a large part in atherosclerosis: they proliferate when stimulated and synthesize collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, growth factors and cytokines.

cards.t: Intimal thickening (the neointimal response to injury)
q: what is the neointimal response
how does a vessel respond to injury
why does vascular injury narrow the lumen
cards.x:
The neointimal response is the vessel wall's standard reaction to injury: when there is endothelial dysfunction or loss, smooth muscle cells are recruited into the intima (the inner layer) and multiply there. This happens with any form of vascular damage, regardless of the cause.

The steps: endothelial cells migrate in from uninjured areas (or come from precursor cells in the blood) and nitric oxide production falls. Smooth muscle cells, or circulating precursors, migrate into the intima, proliferate and synthesize extracellular matrix, which is the primary pathology of neointimal hyperplasia. Platelets activate so a thrombus forms, and leukocytes are recruited so the inflammatory cascade begins.

The result is a thickened intima that narrows the lumen and compromises flow, with wall remodeling and loss of lumen patency (openness). Excessive thickening can cause stenosis and obstruction.

cards.t: Why falling nitric oxide matters after vessel injury
q: what does nitric oxide do in blood vessels
why does losing nitric oxide matter after injury
cards.x:
When the vessel lining is injured, nitric oxide production falls. Nitric oxide is a vasodilator (it relaxes the vessel) and an inhibitor of platelet adhesion, so losing it shifts the vessel toward constriction and thrombosis.

It is a twofold problem: the injured vessel is narrowed by the thickened intima and also constricted because the dilating signal has been lost.

cards.t: Narrowing versus weakening, and which size of artery gets which disease
k: aneurysm atherosclerosis hypertension by vessel size
q: what are the principal mechanisms of vascular disease
which vessels get atherosclerosis and which get aneurysms
how does disease depend on artery size
cards.x:
Vascular disease works by two principal mechanisms. One is narrowing, which is stenosis or obstruction of the lumen, either progressive (atherosclerosis) or precipitous (thrombosis, embolism). The other is weakening, which leads to dilation or rupture. A gradual narrowing allows collateral supply to develop, while a sudden one does not.

Each vessel type is built for its own physiologic needs, so each size of artery tends to be tied to one typical pattern of disease (the patterns overlap; for example, atherosclerosis also affects the aorta):
- Large (elastic) arteries, such as the aorta (about 2 to 3.5 cm) and its major branches like the iliac arteries: aneurysm, from weakening with loss of elastic tissue.
- Medium (muscular) arteries, such as the coronary arteries (3 to 4 mm) and renal arteries: atherosclerosis, narrowing by intimal thickening.
- Small arteries (2 mm or less) and arterioles (20 to 100 micrometers): hypertension, with mechanical stress, endothelial dysfunction, less elasticity and weakening while the lumen stiffens and narrows.

cards.t: How blood pressure is determined and regulated
q: what determines blood pressure
how does sodium raise blood pressure
what regulates vascular resistance
cards.x:
Blood pressure is set by two things: cardiac output and vascular resistance (blood pressure equals cardiac output times peripheral resistance).

Resistance is regulated at the arterioles, by neural and hormonal input, as a balance of vasoconstrictors (such as angiotensin) and vasodilators (such as nitric oxide). Other constrictors include catecholamines, thromboxane, leukotrienes and endothelin. Other dilators include prostaglandins and kinins. Alpha-adrenergic nerve input constricts, and beta-adrenergic input dilates. Local factors such as autoregulation, pH and hypoxia also act.

Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume. It is fed by blood volume (sodium, mineralocorticoids, atrial natriuretic peptide) and by cardiac factors (heart rate, contractility). Blood volume is regulated by sodium excretion or resorption. Water follows sodium. More sodium in the blood pulls in water, raising volume and so pressure. That is one reason chronic high sodium intake contributes to hypertension.

q: what happens when blood pressure falls
what does renin do
how does angiotensin II raise blood pressure
cards.x:
This is the body's response to a fall in blood pressure, and it runs in a chain.

- The kidneys secrete renin in response to decreased pressure in the afferent arterioles (the small vessels feeding the kidney's filters).
- Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
- The endothelium converts this into angiotensin II, a vasoconstrictor.
- Angiotensin II raises pressure by increasing smooth muscle tone and by increasing the adrenal secretion of aldosterone, which increases renal sodium resorption.

So the response tightens the vessels and also holds on to sodium (and with it water) to raise volume.

q: what causes hypertension
what is renovascular hypertension
what is the difference between primary and secondary hypertension
cards.x:
Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure. It is a common disorder. It is a risk factor for atherosclerosis, congestive heart failure, renal failure, cerebral hemorrhage and aortic dissection.

- Primary (idiopathic) hypertension is 90 to 95% of cases. It comes from genetic plus environmental factors, with suspected small changes in renal sodium homeostasis and/or vessel wall tone and structure. The chain: insufficient renal sodium excretion at normal arterial pressure leads to more fluid volume, then more cardiac output, then more vasoconstriction, then raised pressure.
- Secondary hypertension is much less common. In the renovascular form, renal artery stenosis lowers glomerular flow and afferent arteriolar pressure. That induces renin secretion and raises volume and vessel tone. Primary hyperaldosteronism is a common cause, for example from an adrenal adenoma (a benign adrenal tumor).

q: what is arteriosclerosis
what are the types of arteriosclerosis
what is Monckeberg medial sclerosis
cards.x:
Arteriosclerosis is literally hardening of the arteries: the generic term for arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity. It comes in four patterns.

- Arteriolosclerosis, of small arteries and arterioles, can cause downstream ischemic injury. It has two subtypes, both related to hypertension. In the hyaline type the wall is thickened by protein deposition and looks glassy pink, with the lumen markedly narrowed. In the hyperplastic type, concentric layers of smooth muscle cells ("onion skinning") obliterate the lumen.
- Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia, in muscular arteries larger than arterioles, is driven by inflammation or mechanical injury and is a healing response. Vessels can become very stenotic (for example in-stent restenosis, narrowing again inside a stent). It is a major long-term limitation of solid-organ transplants.
- Monckeberg medial sclerosis is calcification of the media of muscular arteries and is usually not clinically significant.
- Atherosclerosis (Greek for gruel and hardening) is the most clinically relevant form.

q: what are the risk factors for atherosclerosis
what is lipoprotein(a)
why are men and postmenopausal women at higher risk
cards.x:
Atherosclerosis is the major cause of coronary, cerebral and peripheral vascular disease. It causes more illness and death in the Western world than any other disorder. Older sources put it at about half of all deaths, but cardiovascular disease accounts for roughly a third of US deaths today. The risk factors are acquired, inherited, sex-related or age-related.

- Hyperlipidemia, smoking, hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
- Lipoprotein(a): an altered form of low-density lipoprotein whose risk is independent of total cholesterol.
- Metabolic syndrome: central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension and dyslipidemia, which induce a hypercoagulable and proinflammatory state.
- Inflammation (C-reactive protein), now included in cardiovascular risk stratification.
- Genetics: family history is a strong risk factor, classically taught as the most important one.
- Increasing age: progressive, manifesting in the 40s to 60s and rising by decade.
- Sex and hormones: men and postmenopausal women are the higher-risk groups, with a likely protective effect of estrogen.

cards.t: Atherosclerosis as a chronic inflammatory and healing response
q: what is the sequence of events in atherosclerosis
why is atherosclerosis called a chronic inflammatory response
when does a plaque calcify
cards.x:
Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury. In order:

- A healthy vessel is injured (think of the risk factors).
- Low-density lipoprotein accumulates in the wall.
- Monocytes adhere to the endothelium.
- Platelets adhere.
- Smooth muscle cells are recruited, by factors released from activated platelets and macrophages.
- Smooth muscle proliferates, extracellular matrix is produced and T cells are recruited.
- Lipid accumulates.
- Matrix and necrotic debris calcify.

The last two steps are lipid accumulation and then calcification.

cards.t: The atheroma: cap and necrotic center
q: what is an atheroma
what is inside an atherosclerotic plaque
what do stable and unstable plaques do
cards.x:
An atheroma is an intimal lesion that projects into the lumen, with a soft lipid core under a fibrous cap. The fibrous cap contains smooth muscle cells, macrophages, foam cells, lymphocytes, collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and new blood vessels (neovascularization). The necrotic center holds cell debris, cholesterol crystals, foam cells and calcium.

What it does depends on stability: stable plaques cause ischemia, while unstable ones rupture, thrombose and embolize.

q: what is peripheral arterial disease
why does claudication happen
how is claudication like stable angina
cards.x:
Peripheral arterial disease is a consequence of atherosclerosis: the arteries become stenotic, which causes ischemia. When metabolic demand increases, as with walking, the patient develops claudication, caused by a lack of oxygenated blood to the working muscle.

The idea is the same as in stable angina: a fixed narrowing that shows itself when demand rises.

q: what is the difference between an aneurysm and a dissection
what is a false aneurysm
what does saccular versus fusiform mean
cards.x:
An aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilation of a vessel, congenital or acquired, classified by shape. A dissection is blood entering a defect in the arterial wall and tunneling through the medial or medial-adventitial planes. So the wall is split into layers rather than merely dilated.

- True aneurysm, saccular: a focal outward bulge (the berry shape).
- True aneurysm, fusiform: circumferential dilation.
- False aneurysm: the wall has ruptured and the hematoma is held in only by extravascular connective tissue.
- Dissection: a tear in the intima lets blood split the media.

cards.t: What weakens the vessel wall in aneurysm and dissection
q: why do aneurysms form
how does Marfan syndrome cause aneurysm or dissection
cards.x:
Arterial walls are constantly remodeling. So anything that compromises the connective tissue of the wall, in structure or function, can produce an aneurysm or dissection.

- Poor connective tissue quality: defective collagen synthesis, or abnormal transforming growth factor signaling as in Marfan syndrome.
- Imbalance of collagen degradation and synthesis: altered by inflammation and proteases, with a genetic predisposition in the setting of inflammatory lesions.
- Loss of smooth muscle cells or inappropriate matrix synthesis: caused by ischemia, hypertension or tertiary syphilis.

Predisposing conditions for aortic aneurysm are atherosclerosis, hypertension and smoking.

q: what causes an abdominal aortic aneurysm
when does an aneurysm rupture
what causes a thoracic aortic aneurysm
cards.x:
An aortic aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilation of the aorta caused by a weakened wall, and where it sits points to the likely cause. Rupture is a separate danger, and its risk rises with size.

- Abdominal aortic aneurysm: atherosclerotic aneurysms occur most commonly in the abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries. Rupture risk rises with size: under 4 cm they typically do not rupture, and over 5.5 cm the risk is very high.
- Thoracic aortic aneurysm: commonly associated with hypertension, and also with Marfan syndrome and inflammation. A bicuspid aortic valve raises local hemodynamic stress.

q: what is a berry aneurysm
what causes a mycotic aneurysm
what is the main feature of a saccular aneurysm
cards.x:
Aneurysms differ in shape and in cause. Three types:

- Saccular (berry): thin-walled protrusions with very thin or absent media and an absent or fragmented internal elastic lamina, typically acquired. The causes are multifactorial: hemodynamic stress, turbulent flow causing structural fatigue, hypertension, smoking, connective tissue disease and possibly inflammation. The lack of elastic lamina is the main feature.
- Fusiform: dilation of the entire circumference, where atherosclerosis may be a factor.
- Mycotic: usually from infected emboli in infective endocarditis. It is rare.

q: what is aortic dissection
what is the main risk factor for aortic dissection
who gets an aortic dissection
cards.x:
In aortic dissection, blood enters a defect in the arterial wall and tunnels through the laminar planes of the media. It splits them to form a blood-filled channel inside the wall. So the wall is split into layers rather than simply dilated, as it is in an aneurysm.

Hypertension is the major risk factor. Two groups are affected: people aged 40 to 60 with hypertension, and younger patients with connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome. A sudden pressure spike (cocaine) or injury during catheterization can also lead to one.

q: what is fibromuscular dysplasia
what is the string of beads sign
cards.x:
Fibromuscular dysplasia is a focal irregular thickening of medium and large muscular arteries. Its exact cause is unknown. Segments of the wall are thickened by hyperplasia and fibrosis of the media and intima, causing luminal stenosis. The renal arteries are an example (and in the renal arteries it can cause renovascular hypertension).

The angiographic sign is a "string of beads", alternating narrowing and dilation along the vessel. It may lead to aneurysmal dilation that can rupture.

q: what is vasculitis
how is vasculitis classified
which vasculitis affects large vessels
cards.x:
Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall, with manifestations set by the vessel affected. It can involve any organ or vessel but mostly small vessels. There are about 20 primary forms. There are two main pathogenic mechanisms: immune-mediated inflammation, and direct invasion of the wall by infectious pathogens.

By vessel size:
- Large: giant cell arteritis (granulomatous inflammation of the carotid, vertebral and temporal arteries).
- Medium: polyarteritis nodosa, and Kawasaki disease (an acute febrile illness of children under 5).
- Small: two subgroups. One is anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated necrotizing vasculitis. The other is immune complex vasculitis, as in systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.

q: what is Raynaud phenomenon
why do fingers go white then blue then red
what causes the color changes in Raynaud
cards.x:
Raynaud phenomenon is an exaggerated vasoconstrictive response to cold and emotional stress, mostly in the arteries and arterioles of the extremities. Vasoconstriction leads to tissue anoxia (no oxygen). The return of oxygenated blood produces the color sequence white, then blue, then red.

Each color has a reason: white from the constriction, blue from the lack of oxygen, and red when flow returns. That return is painful because of rapid vessel dilation and a rush of inflammatory signals.

q: what is an arteriovenous fistula
what causes an arteriovenous fistula
why is an arteriovenous fistula made for dialysis
cards.x:
An arteriovenous fistula is an irregular direct connection between an artery and a vein that bypasses the capillaries. It can arise from developmental defects or rupture of an arterial aneurysm into an adjacent vein. It can also arise from a penetrating injury that pierces both artery and vein, or inflammatory necrosis of adjacent vessels.

It can also be created surgically for hemodialysis access, to carry high flow at a rapid rate. The vein then remodels until its wall can withstand arterial pressure.

cards.t: Varicose veins, esophageal varices and hemorrhoids
q: what causes varicose veins
what are esophageal varices
why do varicose veins affect the legs
cards.x:
Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous veins caused by chronic high intraluminal pressure (pressure inside the vein) and weakened wall support. They come from insufficiency of the venous valves, which normally prevent gravitational reverse flow. When a valve is damaged, blood falls back and the vein below it balloons. They usually affect the lower extremities (flow there runs against gravity), in the superficial great and small saphenous veins. Veins have larger diameters and lumens than arteries and a thinner media, which allows greater capacitance (they can hold more blood).

Related varicosities: esophageal varices are dilated submucosal distal esophageal veins from cirrhosis and portal venous hypertension. Hemorrhoids are varicose dilations of the venous plexus at the anorectal junction. Varicose veins and hemorrhoids are both linked to pregnancy.

q: what is deep vein thrombosis
what are the causes of deep vein thrombosis
how does a deep vein clot cause a pulmonary embolus
cards.x:
Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep vein, typically of the legs, and it is the third most common cause of death from cardiovascular disease. It arises in the deep veins (femoral, popliteal, tibial) where stasis in a dilated vein leads to thrombosis.

Causes and risk factors:
- Reduced blood flow: immobility, such as bed rest, general anesthesia, the postoperative state, stroke or a long flight.
- Increased venous pressure: mechanical compression or functional impairment.
- Mechanical injury: trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use.
- Increased blood viscosity: dehydration, thrombocytosis.
- Increased coagulation (genetic or acquired): cancer, sepsis, systemic lupus erythematosus, oral estrogen.

Over weeks, neutrophils and macrophages infiltrate the fibrin clot and collagen gradually replaces the fibrin, which decreases blood flow. If the thrombus dislodges, it becomes an embolus that travels through the venous system to the pulmonary artery and occludes it: a pulmonary embolus.

q: what is the Virchow triad
what are the three causes of thrombosis
cards.x:
Virchow triad names the three factors behind thrombosis (clot formation inside a vessel): (1) damage to the vessel wall, (2) abnormal blood flow, meaning turbulence or stasis (pooling), and (3) hypercoagulability (blood that clots too easily).

Triggers are multifactorial, with the three involved in varying degrees. You can see them in deep vein thrombosis: immobility changes the flow, trauma or surgery injures the wall, and cancer or oral estrogen makes the blood clot more readily.

q: what are the three functions of immunity
what is the difference between the immune response and immunity
cards.x:
The immune response is the set of cellular defense reactions the body uses to protect itself against threats. Immunity is the resulting state of protection, and it does three jobs:
- Defense: resisting invaders such as microbes.
- Surveillance: watching the body's own cells for mutant or cancerous ones.
- Homeostasis: clearing away cellular debris.

The point of the list is that immunity is not only about infection. The same system that fights a bacterium also polices your own cells and tidies up dead material.

cards.t: How lymph moves through lymphatic vessels
q: how does lymph move without a pump
how does fluid get into lymphatic capillaries
cards.x:
The lymphatic system has no heart of its own, so lymph is pushed along by the body around it. Skeletal muscle movement, the pressure changes in the chest during breathing and the pulsing of nearby arteries all squeeze the vessels, and physical activity or even passive movement keeps lymph flowing.

Valves make that squeezing one-way. In a lymphatic capillary the endothelial cells overlap like flaps: interstitial fluid pushes between their edges to get in, and the flaps close so it cannot get back out. Larger lymphatic vessels have smooth muscle and internal valves of their own. Think of it as a series of one-way doors that turn any squeeze into forward flow.

q: what is the difference between humoral and cellular immunity
which cells do humoral immunity
cards.x:
These are the two arms of the adaptive immune response, split by what does the work.
- Humoral immunity works through antibodies (immunoglobulins). B cells turn into plasma cells, and the plasma cells are the cells that actually make the antibodies.
- Cellular immunity works through T cells themselves. Killer T cells (CD8, cytotoxic T cells) destroy virus-infected cells, tumor cells and transplanted cells, and releasing perforin is an important part of how they do it.

Quick way to keep them apart: humoral means something dissolved in body fluid (antibody) does the job; cellular means a cell has to make contact and kill.

q: what are the steps of phagocytosis
what is a phagolysosome
cards.x:
Phagocytosis is how a cell such as a macrophage eats a microbe. It runs in five steps:
- The microbe sticks to the phagocyte.
- The phagocyte reaches around it with pseudopods (arm-like extensions) and engulfs it into a bubble called a phagosome.
- The phagosome fuses with a lysosome, making a phagolysosome.
- Lysosomal enzymes (acid hydrolases) kill and digest the microbe, leaving a residual body.
- Whatever cannot be digested is pushed back out by exocytosis.

The key move is the fusion: the microbe is first trapped, then delivered to the cell's digestive enzymes.

q: what is an epitope
what is immunologic memory
how is adaptive immunity specific
cards.x:
Memory means that the second time the body meets an antigen, the adaptive response is faster and stronger than the first time.

Specificity means the adaptive system recognizes exact targets. B-cell and T-cell receptors each recognize a particular epitope, the small part of an antigen a receptor actually fits. Innate receptors are less picky: they recognize patterns shared by whole groups of organisms. So innate immunity knows roughly what kind of invader it is facing, while adaptive immunity knows exactly which one.

cards.t: Active versus passive immunity (natural and artificial)
q: what is the difference between active and passive immunity
is a vaccine active or passive immunity
what is natural passive immunity
cards.x:
Two questions sort every example.

First, who made the antibodies? In active immunity your own body responds after exposure to the antigen. In passive immunity you receive preformed antibodies from another source. Passive protection starts immediately but fades as the transferred antibodies are lost.

Second, how did the exposure happen? Natural means it happened in the course of life; artificial means it was done on purpose.
- Active natural: meeting the antigen naturally.
- Active artificial: vaccination.
- Passive natural: maternal immunoglobulin G (IgG) through the placenta and IgA in breast milk.
- Passive artificial: tetanus or rabies immune globulin.

q: what is innate immunity
what is part of the innate immune system
cards.x:
Innate immunity is the set of defenses that work without any earlier sensitization to a particular antigen. It does not need to have met the invader before. Instead it recognizes conserved microbial patterns (features many microbes share) and signs of cell injury.

It includes skin and mucosal barriers, phagocytes, complement and interferons. Natural killer cells provide its cell-killing arm and make up roughly 5 to 15% of circulating lymphocytes. Host characteristics also add a species-specific resistance.

q: what do neutrophils do
what are eosinophils for
what is the difference between a basophil and a mast cell
cards.x:
Granulocytes are white cells with visible granules. There are three:
- Neutrophils ("polys", polymorphonuclear leukocytes) do phagocytosis. They are the first responders and the most numerous.
- Eosinophils deal with allergic reactions and parasitic invasion.
- Basophils are similar to tissue mast cells.

A handy way to keep the last two apart: basophils circulate in the blood (baso, B, blood), while mast cells sit in the tissues.

q: what is the difference between a monocyte and a macrophage
what is a histiocyte
cards.x:
A monocyte and a macrophage are the same cell line in two places. Monocytes circulate in the blood and move into tissues during inflammation, where tissue signals turn them into macrophages. Some resident macrophages are different: they develop before birth and renew themselves locally.

Macrophages remove material and coordinate inflammatory responses. A histiocyte is simply another name for a tissue macrophage. Monocytes and lymphocytes together are the agranulocytes, the white cells without obvious granules.

cards.t: T cells, B cells and natural killer cells compared
q: what is the difference between T cells and B cells
where do T cells mature
how are natural killer cells different from cytotoxic T cells
cards.x:
All three lymphocytes come from hematopoietic stem cells, but they mature in different places and do different jobs.
- T cells mature in the thymus and run adaptive cellular immunity. Their receptor is the T-cell receptor.
- B cells mature in the bone marrow and run adaptive humoral immunity. Their receptor is surface immunoglobulin, which they lose when they become plasma cells.
- Natural killer cells are innate killers. Unlike cytotoxic T cells they do not need to recognize a specific antigen, and they target tumor cells and many infectious microbes.

Only T and B cells form conventional memory cells.

cards.t: Antigens and how they start an immune response
q: what is an antigen
how does an antigen trigger an immune response
cards.x:
An antigen is something the immune system can recognize, and the particular part a B-cell or T-cell receptor recognizes is called an epitope. Antigens come in different types, such as soluble toxin molecules, viruses and bacteria, and the type decides what antibody binding can achieve.

An antigen starts a response by selecting the cells that fit it. Exposure to the antigen starts the antigen-dependent phase of B-cell maturation: the antigen picks out the matching B cell, which multiplies (clonal expansion) into antibody-making plasma cells and memory cells. T cells see antigen differently: helper T cells recognize antigen pieces presented on major histocompatibility complex class II, and cytotoxic T cells on class I.

q: what is the difference between the primary and secondary immune response
why is the second exposure response faster
what does a high IgM mean
cards.x:
The primary response follows the first exposure to an antigen. Antibody builds up over days, and immunoglobulin M (IgM) rises first, with IgG following later and lower. Memory cells are made during this response.

The secondary response follows re-exposure. Because memory cells are already waiting, it is generally faster and stronger, and class-switched antibody, often IgG, reaches higher levels and lasts longer.

That pattern can be read backwards: a high IgM suggests this is the first exposure, while a low IgM with a high IgG suggests the person has met the antigen before.

cards.t: How a B cell becomes a plasma cell
q: how does a B cell turn into a plasma cell
what are the phases of B cell maturation
what is clonal selection
cards.x:
B-cell maturation has two phases. In the antigen-independent phase the B cell puts immunoglobulin M on its surface as its receptor. In the antigen-dependent phase, which exposure to the antigen starts, the B cell differentiates into a plasma cell that makes specific antibody.

The antigen does the choosing: from the whole repertoire of B cells it selects the one whose receptor fits, and that cell divides (clonal expansion) into plasma cells that secrete antibody and memory cells for next time. Helper (CD4) T cells support the process, while the plasma cells do the actual secreting. B cells lose their surface immunoglobulin when they become plasma cells.

cards.t: Antibody structure: heavy and light chains, Fab and Fc
q: what is the structure of an antibody
what is the difference between Fab and Fc
what determines antibody class
cards.x:
The basic antibody unit is a Y made of two heavy chains and two light chains held together by disulfide bonds. Light chains come in two kinds, kappa or lambda.

The two ends do different jobs. At the tips of the arms, the variable regions of a heavy and a light chain together form the antigen-binding site; the arm is the Fab fragment. The stem is the Fc fragment, made of heavy-chain constant regions, and it handles effector functions such as binding complement and cells. The heavy-chain constant region also decides the antibody's class.

So Fab grabs the target and Fc decides what happens next. The enzyme papain cuts immunoglobulin G at the hinge into two Fab pieces and the Fc.

cards.t: The five antibody classes (IgM, IgG, IgA, IgD, IgE)
q: what are the five types of antibodies
which antibody crosses the placenta
which antibody is a pentamer
cards.x:
The five classes differ in their heavy-chain constant region, which changes their shape and job:
- IgM: secreted as a pentamer (five units); often the first class made in a new response; good at clumping and at starting complement.
- IgG: the most abundant, about 75 to 80% of serum antibody; crosses the placenta, which is how a mother protects her baby; prominent in secondary responses.
- IgA: a dimer in secretions such as saliva, tears and colostrum; stops microbes attaching at mucosal surfaces.
- IgD: on many mature naive B cells with IgM, as part of their receptor.
- IgE: bound to mast cells and basophils; drives immediate allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, and fights some parasites.

q: what is serum protein electrophoresis
where do antibodies run on electrophoresis
cards.x:
Electrophoresis separates serum proteins by how they move in an electric field. They split into albumin, which runs nearest the positive pole, and the alpha, beta and gamma globulin fractions, with gamma nearest the negative pole.

Immunofixation goes a step further and identifies which immunoglobulin heavy-chain and light-chain types are present.

cards.t: What antibodies do: five ways they stop antigens
q: how do antibodies destroy antigens
what is the difference between agglutination and precipitation
what does neutralization mean
cards.x:
Antibodies bind antigens and stop their harmful behavior in several ways:
- Agglutination: clumping. When the antigens sit on cell surfaces, antibodies link the cells together.
- Neutralization: binding blocks an essential interaction with a host cell, such as a virus attaching or a toxin reaching its target. It works without destroying the particle.
- Lysis: destroying the cell, by bringing in the complement system.
- Precipitation: cross-linking soluble antigens into larger complexes that fall out of solution and are easier for phagocytes to clear.
- Opsonization: coating antigen on a cell surface so a phagocyte can ingest it more easily.

The antigen type decides which fits: a toxin is neutralized and precipitated, a virus neutralized and agglutinated, a bacterium opsonized.

q: why is O the universal donor
who can a type A person receive blood from
why do mismatched transfusions agglutinate
cards.x:
Red cells carry A antigen, B antigen, both or neither, and plasma usually carries antibodies against whichever antigens the person lacks. Give red cells carrying an antigen the recipient has antibodies against and the cells agglutinate.
- O: neither antigen; anti-A and anti-B; receives O only.
- A: A antigen; anti-B; receives O or A.
- B: B antigen; anti-A; receives O or B.
- AB (both antigens): neither antibody; receives any of the four groups.

Group O red cells carry neither antigen, which is why O is called the universal donor. This is the ABO (blood group) red-cell picture only: Rh status, other antibodies and compatibility testing also matter, and plasma compatibility works differently.

k: natural killer cell killing antibody-coated cells
q: what is antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity
how do natural killer cells use antibodies
cards.x:
Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is antibody and a killer cell working as a team. Immunoglobulin G coats an infected cell with its antigen-binding ends holding the target, which leaves the Fc stem pointing outward. A natural killer cell binds that exposed Fc through its CD16 (cluster of differentiation 16) receptor and kills the cell.

The antibody supplies the recognition; the responding cell supplies the killing.

cards.t: CD4 helper versus CD8 cytotoxic T cells
q: what is the difference between CD4 and CD8 T cells
what do helper T cells do
how do cytotoxic T cells kill
cards.x:
Helper T cells carry the marker CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) and recognize antigen pieces presented on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II. They coordinate both arms of the response through cytokines and cell contact: their signals help B cells become antibody-making cells, and interferon gamma from them activates macrophages.

Cytotoxic T cells carry CD8 (cluster of differentiation 8) and recognize antigen pieces on MHC class I. They kill infected or malignant host cells, using perforin and granzymes to trigger the target cell's apoptosis (programmed death).

Memory trick: there are four letters in "help", so CD4 is the helper. And 4 times II equals 8 times I, which pairs CD4 with class II and CD8 with class I.

q: what do regulatory T cells do
what is self-tolerance
cards.x: Regulatory T cells are the brakes of the immune system. They limit immune activation and maintain self-tolerance, the state in which the immune system leaves the body's own tissues alone. Many of them are CD4 (helper-type) cells that express a marker called FOXP3 (the regulatory T-cell marker).

q: what is hypersensitivity
what are the four types of hypersensitivity
is type I the most severe
cards.x:
Hypersensitivity is when an immune reaction, humoral or cellular, ends up injuring the body. There are four types, and the number names a mechanism, not a severity, so type IV is not worse than type I.
- Type I: immunoglobulin E on mast cells releases histamine (allergy, anaphylaxis).
- Type II: antibody binds antigen that is part of a cell or tissue.
- Type III: antigen and antibody form complexes that deposit in tissues and vessel walls.
- Type IV: sensitized T cells do the damage, commonly over 24 to 72 hours.

Ask which of the four is doing the damage and the examples follow.

q: how does type 1 hypersensitivity work
what happens in anaphylaxis
why does a second exposure cause the allergic reaction
cards.x:
Type I is the immediate, IgE-driven reaction. It needs a first exposure to sensitize: the antigen triggers production of immunoglobulin E, which circulates and then becomes fixed on the surface of mast cells and basophils. On the next exposure the antigen binds that surface antibody and the mast cells release mediators such as histamine.

Locally that causes swelling and vasodilation. Anaphylaxis is the rapid, whole-body version, where even a small exposure can cause severe disease: bronchospasm, swelling of the larynx and low blood pressure, although shock and skin findings are not present in every case. Triggers include drugs, insect venoms and other allergens.

q: what is type 2 hypersensitivity
what are examples of type II hypersensitivity
cards.x:
In type II, immunoglobulin G or M binds antigens that are part of a cell or a tissue. The damage then comes through phagocytosis, complement or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Sometimes the antibody does not destroy the cell at all but stimulates or blocks a receptor on it, changing how the cell works.

Examples are ABO (blood group) incompatibility and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, which can cause glomerulonephritis and bleeding in the lungs. Quick way to tell it from type III: in type II the antibody binds antigen sitting on the cell or tissue itself; in type III, antibody and antigen form a complex first and the complex lodges somewhere.

q: what is type 3 hypersensitivity
how do immune complexes cause damage
what is the Arthus reaction
cards.x:
Type III is immune complex disease. Antigen and antibody join into complexes that deposit in tissues or vessel walls, and complement plus recruited inflammatory cells cause the injury where they land.
- Arthus reaction: a local version in someone already sensitized.
- Serum sickness: a whole-body version from circulating complexes, triggered by foreign proteins, drugs or biologic therapies.
- Lupus and immune-complex glomerulonephritis or arthritis are further examples.

The damage follows the complexes, which is why it shows up in places like the kidney and joints rather than at one targeted cell.

q: what is type 4 hypersensitivity
why is type IV hypersensitivity delayed
cards.x:
Type IV is the only type driven by T cells instead of antibodies. Sensitized CD4 (helper) or CD8 (cytotoxic) T cells mediate it, and common reactions take 24 to 72 hours to develop, which is why it is called delayed (timing varies). The T cells release cytokines that recruit and activate inflammatory cells, and cytotoxic T cells can injure target cells directly. Persistent stimulation can produce granulomas in some settings.

Examples are contact dermatitis, tuberculosis-related reactions and T cell-mediated transplant rejection.

cards.t: The complement system and what it does
q: what is the complement system
what does complement do
does complement always cause lysis
cards.x:
Complement is a network of proteins, many of them made by the liver, that circulate in an inactive form. Once something activates the first one, a regulated cascade follows, so one small signal can produce a large response.

It has three main outcomes:
- Opsonization: coating particles with complement protein (C3b) so phagocytes eat them quickly.
- Inflammation: some pieces (C3a, C4a, C5a) dilate vessels so more immune cells arrive, and some attract neutrophils and macrophages.
- Lysis: the membrane attack complex punches holes in a target cell.

Lysis is only one possible outcome, so complement can be active even when no cells are being burst.

cards.t: Classical, lectin and alternative complement pathways
q: what are the three complement pathways
what starts the classical pathway
where do the complement pathways meet
cards.x:
Three different starting points lead into the same cascade:
- Classical: usually starts when C1 (the first complement component) recognizes immunoglobulin M or G already bound to antigen (some classical activation does not need antibody).
- Lectin: recognition proteins such as mannose-binding lectin bind carbohydrates on microbes and activate proteases attached to them.
- Alternative: C3 (complement component 3) activates and amplifies on permissive surfaces, helped by factor B, factor D and properdin.

All three converge on C3 activation, then C5 (complement component 5), and C5b goes on to build the membrane attack complex. Think of three on-ramps merging onto one highway at C3.

q: what is the membrane attack complex
how does complement lyse cells
cards.x: The membrane attack complex is complement's hole-punch. C5b starts the assembly of the last components, C6 (complement component 6) through C9 (complement component 9), and multiple C9 units form a channel through a susceptible membrane. The pore wrecks the cell's ionic and osmotic balance, and severe disruption bursts the cell (lysis).

q: what is autoimmunity
what are examples of autoimmune disease
how do autoantibodies cause disease
cards.x:
Autoimmunity is the immune system acting against the body's own tissues. Normally self-tolerance is actively maintained, and regulatory T cells are a key part of that, limiting immune activation.

When antibody targets self it can work in two ways: destroying the cell it binds, or stimulating or blocking a receptor without destroying the cell (both are type II mechanisms). Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease is a type II example, and lupus with immune-complex glomerulonephritis or arthritis is a type III example. Autoantibodies also become more common with age, and clinical findings decide whether they matter.

q: what is the difference between primary and secondary immunodeficiency
what is X-linked agammaglobulinemia
what is DiGeorge syndrome
cards.x:
Primary immunodeficiency is an intrinsic defect in how the immune system develops or works, often with a genetic basis. Secondary immunodeficiency is reduced function caused by something else: disease, medications, malignancy or inadequate nutrition.

Three primary examples, sorted by which arm fails:
- X-linked agammaglobulinemia: B cells fail to mature, antibodies are very low, so recurrent pyogenic (pus-forming) bacterial infections follow.
- DiGeorge syndrome: variable impairment of thymus and T-cell development.
- Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID): profound T-cell failure plus impaired B-cell immunity; it may show up in early infancy or on newborn screening.

cards.t: How age affects the immune system
q: how does aging affect the immune system
how are newborns protected from infection
cards.x:
Both ends of life are vulnerable, for different reasons. Newborns have a still-developing immune system and lean on borrowed protection: maternal immunoglobulin G that crossed the placenta and IgA from breast milk. That maternal antibody protection declines over time, at rates that vary by antibody and exposure.

In older adults, changes in lymphocyte function and in the range of receptors can weaken responses to new antigens. Autoantibodies also become more common with age, and clinical findings decide whether they matter.

cards.t: The respiratory membrane and the alveolar cells
q: what is the respiratory membrane
which cells make surfactant
what layers do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross
cards.x:
The respiratory membrane is the thin barrier between the air in an alveolus and the blood in its capillary, and gas exchange happens across it. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse through six thin layers: the alveolar fluid with surfactant, the alveolar epithelium, its basement membrane, the interstitial space, the capillary basement membrane and the capillary endothelium.

Two cell types line the alveolus. Type I pneumocytes form the thin wall that gas crosses. Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant. An alveolar macrophage sits in the air space as a defender.

cards.t: Normal pulmonary circulation: high flow, low pressure
q: what is normal pulmonary artery pressure
why is the pulmonary circulation low pressure
cards.x:
The pulmonary circulation normally handles a lot of blood at low pressure: it is a high-flow, low-pressure system. A healthy adult's pulmonary arterial pressure is about 22/8 to 25/8 mmHg, with a mean of about 15 mmHg.

Keeping that baseline in mind is what makes pulmonary hypertension make sense: the same flow at a much higher pressure means something is narrowing or blocking the vessels, or pushing back from the left side of the heart.

cards.t: Starling forces: how fluid moves across a capillary
q: why does fluid leave the capillary at the arterial end
what increases capillary filtration
what is oncotic pressure
cards.x:
Two kinds of pressure fight over the fluid in a capillary. Hydrostatic pressure, the push of the blood itself, drives fluid out. Colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure, the pull of plasma proteins, draws fluid back in. The Starling relation sums them: net filtration = Kf[(Pc - Pif) - (πc - πif)].

Along the capillary, hydrostatic pressure falls while osmotic pressure stays about the same. In one textbook example the arterial end has 35 mm of hydrostatic pressure against 25 mm of osmotic pull, so 10 mm pushes fluid out; at the venous end hydrostatic pressure is down to 15 mm, so osmotic pull wins and 10 mm draws fluid back in. Anything that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure or lowers plasma oncotic pressure tips the balance toward fluid leaving the vessel.

q: what is the difference between hypoxemia and hypoxia
is hypoxemia the same as hypoxia
cards.x: Hypoxemia is a low oxygen level in the blood, measured as a low arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) and a low hemoglobin saturation, by arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry. Hypoxia is decreased oxygenation of the tissues. The "-emia" ending means blood, so hypoxemia is about what the blood carries and hypoxia is about what the tissues receive.

cards.t: Acute respiratory failure: the blood gas definition
q: what defines acute respiratory failure
what PaO2 is respiratory failure
what is the difference between hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure
what causes hypercapnic respiratory failure
what is the difference between dead space and shunt
cards.x:
