Hypoxic respiratory failure is a failure of oxygenation: oxygen is low while carbon dioxide is normal or low. Its mechanisms are ventilation/perfusion mismatch, shunt, decreased diffusion, alveolar hypoventilation and high altitude.

Hypercapnic (hypercarbic) ventilatory failure is a failure to remove carbon dioxide, so it builds up. Ventilation is too low for the carbon dioxide being made: a low breathing rate, nerves that cannot signal the muscles (Guillain-Barre syndrome, spinal cord injury), increased dead space (pulmonary embolism, low cardiac output, hypovolemia), more carbon dioxide production (fever, infection, trauma, burns) or an inability to sense a high carbon dioxide (drugs, alkalosis).

Dead space versus shunt: dead space is ventilation without enough perfusion, wasted breathing; shunt is perfusion without enough ventilation.

q: what causes acute respiratory failure
how can neuromuscular disease cause respiratory failure
cards.x:
The causes sort by where along the breathing chain the problem sits:
- Central nervous system: sedatives, stroke, brain trauma or tumor.
- Neuromuscular disease: multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, polio, Guillain-Barre syndrome, quadriplegia.
- Chest wall and skeleton: kyphoscoliosis, chest trauma, pleural effusion, massive ascites.
- Airway: laryngospasm, foreign-body aspiration.
- Lung tissue itself: shock, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, advanced emphysema, pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome.

Reading top to bottom follows the signal from the brain, through the nerves and muscles and chest wall, down the airway to the alveoli.

q: what is pulmonary hypertension
what pressure defines pulmonary hypertension
what is idiopathic pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Pulmonary hypertension is abnormally high pressure in the pulmonary arteries of what is normally a high-flow, low-pressure system (normal mean about 15 mmHg). Two definitions are in circulation: older teaching uses a sustained pulmonary arterial pressure above 30 mmHg, while the current hemodynamic definition is a resting mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg, measured by right heart catheterization. Know both.

It comes in two types. Idiopathic pulmonary hypertension has no known cause, is rapidly progressive, is more common in women and appears in the third to fourth decade. Secondary pulmonary hypertension results from a known disease process.

q: what causes pulmonary hypertension
how does mitral stenosis cause pulmonary hypertension
how does COPD cause pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
Pressure is flow times resistance, plus whatever pushes back from downstream, so secondary pulmonary hypertension has three routes:
- More flow or thicker blood: a left-to-right shunt (atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus) or polycythemia.
- More resistance: hypoxic vasoconstriction in chronic bronchitis and advanced emphysema, obstruction from an embolism, or pulmonary fibrosis.
- Higher left atrial pressure backing up into the lungs: mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation or left ventricular failure.

Over time the vessels remodel: the media of the small pulmonary arteries thickens with more muscle (driven by local hypoxia and acidosis), the intima becomes fibrotic, and sustained high pressure produces plexiform lesions, a tangled network of vessels.

q: what are the types of lung cancer
which lung cancer grows fastest
which lung cancer is central
cards.x:
Location and speed separate the four:
- Squamous cell (20-30%): central, two-thirds arising in the central bronchi near the hilus as growth into the airway. Sputum cytology can show it, so it tends to be found earlier. Doubles its volume in about 100 days.
- Adenocarcinoma (35-40%, the largest share): peripheral, so harder to catch early; doubles in about 180 days and spreads to distant organs.
- Large cell (5-10%): peripheral like adenocarcinoma, large cells in nests; doubles in about 100 days.
- Small cell, or oat cell (15-20%): central, compressing the bronchi; the fastest, doubling in about 33 days, with widespread spread common, the most resistant to therapy and linked to paraneoplastic syndrome.

The doubling times are rough teaching figures, not predictions for a given patient.

cards.t: Obstructive lung disease: where the obstruction sits
q: what is obstructive lung disease
what are the types of obstructive lung disease
why do COPD lungs trap air
cards.x:
Obstructive diseases all raise resistance to airflow, and they sort by where the blockage is:
- In the wall of the airway: asthma, acute bronchitis, chronic bronchitis.
- From lost lung tissue or pressure on the outside of the airway: emphysema, enlarged lymph nodes, tumor.
- In the lumen itself: bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis, cystic fibrosis, epiglottitis, croup, a foreign body.

In chronic obstructive lung disease the bronchioles narrow and block with mucus and the alveoli are destroyed, so the lungs do not deflate like normal lungs: air is trapped in the damaged air sacs.

cards.t: The obstructive pattern on pulmonary function testing
q: what does a low FEV1/FVC mean
what pulmonary function changes happen in obstructive disease
what does a low DLCO mean
cards.x:
Three numbers tell the obstructive story:
- A low ratio of FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) to FVC (forced vital capacity) means air cannot get out fast enough: expiratory airflow limitation.
- A high residual volume means the lungs do not empty completely, so air is left behind.
- A reduced DLCO (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide) raises a separate question about gas transfer.

Restriction looks different: there the key finding is a low total lung capacity.

q: what happens in acute bronchitis
why does a cough last after bronchitis
cards.x:
Acute bronchitis is acute inflammation of the trachea and bronchi. Most causes are viral (influenza A or B, parainfluenza, respiratory syncytial virus, coronavirus, rhinovirus, coxsackievirus, adenovirus); others are bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma, Moraxella and Chlamydia pneumoniae, or irritants such as heat, smoke, chemicals and allergic reactions.

The airways become inflamed and narrowed, make more mucus, and lose ciliary function and parts of their ciliated lining. The microbes can leave the airways hyperirritable for a long time, with episodes of bronchospasm, which is why an improving cough can outlast the illness.

q: what is chronic bronchitis
why are chronic bronchitis patients called blue bloaters
how is chronic bronchitis defined
cards.x:
Chronic bronchitis is defined by its cough: mucus hypersecretion with a productive cough for more than 3 months a year in 2 or more successive years, with obstruction that is persistent and irreversible. Smoking causes about 90%.

Chronic inflammation swells and scars the mucosa, enlarges the bronchial glands and goblet cells and thickens the bronchial wall. Mucus mixes with pus into plugs, and the ciliated lining is replaced by squamous cells, so clearance fails. Narrowed, plugged airways worsen ventilation/perfusion mismatch, giving low oxygen and high carbon dioxide.

"Blue bloater" describes the result: blue from cyanosis, bloated from the edema of right-sided heart failure, which follows when hypoxic vasoconstriction causes pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

q: what is emphysema
why do airways collapse in emphysema
how does smoking cause emphysema
cards.x:
Emphysema is destruction of the alveolar walls without fibrosis, with abnormal enlargement of the air sacs at the ends of the airways. Smoking is the main cause (more than 70 pack-years is highly predictive), along with air pollution and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

The damage comes from protein-digesting enzymes (proteases) released by neutrophils and macrophages. Smoking makes it worse twice over: it causes the inflammation that releases them and it inactivates alpha-1 antitrypsin, the enzyme that normally restrains them.

Why airflow drops: the surrounding lung tissue normally pulls the small airways open, like guy ropes on a tent. Lose that radial traction and the airways narrow, resistance rises, air gets trapped and the sacs distend into bullae.

q: what does alpha-1 antitrypsin do
how does alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency cause emphysema
cards.x: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protective enzyme that stops proteolytic breakdown of alveolar tissue, holding back the protein-digesting enzymes that inflammatory cells release. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a hereditary disorder, behind about 1% of emphysema: with the brake missing, those enzymes digest the alveolar walls. Smoking produces a similar imbalance by inactivating the alpha-1 antitrypsin a person does have.

q: what are the types of emphysema
which emphysema is linked to chronic bronchitis
cards.x:
The types are named for which part of the acinus (the cluster of air spaces at the end of a bronchiole) is destroyed:
- Centriacinar (centrilobular): destroys the respiratory bronchioles in the center; associated with chronic bronchitis.
- Panacinar (panlobular): destroys the alveoli throughout.
- Paraseptal: affects the peripheral lobules, the alveolar ducts and sacs.

q: what is bronchiectasis
why does bronchiectasis cause foul sputum
why are children at risk of bronchiectasis
cards.x:
Bronchiectasis is permanent widening of the bronchi because their walls have been destroyed. It is an obstructive, pus-forming disorder. It can be congenital (about half related to cystic fibrosis) or acquired, and children are at higher risk because their soft, elastic bronchi are easily damaged by overinflation and by distention from inflammation or infection.

Recurrent infection and inflammation destroy the walls of the central bronchi and obliterate the peripheral ones. The ciliated lining turns squamous, so clearance fails. The widened airways then act as pockets where infection sits, producing purulent, foul-smelling sputum; Haemophilus influenzae is the most common bacterial cause. A wider bronchus is not a healthier one, and recovering from a flare does not restore the damaged architecture. By shape it is cylindrical, saccular (cavity-like) or fusiform.

q: what is restrictive lung disease
what confirms a restrictive pattern
what are the causes of restrictive lung disease
cards.x:
Restrictive diseases stop the lungs expanding normally. The cause can be in the lung tissue, the pleura, the chest wall or the neuromuscular pump that drives breathing.
- Lung tissue: fibrotic interstitial diseases (diffuse interstitial lung disease, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, occupational lung disease) and atelectatic disorders (acute and infant respiratory distress syndrome).
- Pleural space: pneumothorax, pleural effusion.
- Nerves, muscles, chest wall and obesity: Guillain-Barre syndrome, myasthenia gravis, kyphoscoliosis, flail chest, obstructive sleep apnea.
- Infection or inflammation: pneumonia, tuberculosis, severe acute respiratory syndrome.

On testing, a low forced vital capacity alone does not prove restriction; a low total lung capacity confirms it.

cards.t: Diffuse interstitial lung disease and its three stages
q: what is interstitial lung disease
what are the stages of interstitial lung disease
which stage of interstitial lung disease is reversible
cards.x:
Fibrotic interstitial lung diseases infiltrate the alveolar walls with cells, fluid and connective tissue, and without treatment the inflammation can progress to irreversible fibrosis. Diffuse interstitial lung disease is immune-mediated: it begins with injury to the alveolar lining cells or the capillary endothelium, and the immune reaction thickens the interstitium and adds collagen.

The alveoli pass through three patterns:
- Inflammation: early and reversible; more inflammatory cells and leakier membranes let fluid and debris into the alveoli.
- Fibrosis: fibroblasts multiply and lay down large amounts of collagen, thickening the walls.
- Destruction: the end stage; alveolar walls are lost and excess fibrin leaves stiff, noncompliant lungs, sometimes with large air-filled cysts.

q: what is sarcoidosis
what is the lesion of sarcoidosis
cards.x:
Sarcoidosis is an acute or chronic disease of unknown cause that affects many organs. It starts when alveolar macrophages are activated by an unknown trigger, with abnormal T-cell function. The hallmark lesion is multiple, uniform, noncaseating epithelioid granulomas, compact clusters of immune cells. They are most common in the lymph nodes and lung, and can also appear in the skin, eyes, spleen, liver, kidney and bone marrow. Star-shaped asteroid bodies can be seen inside them.

The acute form typically appears in people in their 20s and 30s, more often women; the chronic form is common in the third to fourth decade.

q: what is hypersensitivity pneumonitis
what type of hypersensitivity is hypersensitivity pneumonitis
cards.x:
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, also called extrinsic allergic alveolitis, is inflammation of the lung tissue caused by inhaling organic material such as wheat weevil, various fungi or bird proteins (parakeet, pigeon, chicken). The names tell the exposure: bird fancier's lung, farmer's lung, mushroom worker's, cheese maker's and fish-meat worker's lung. It is more common in nonsmokers.

The mechanism is type III hypersensitivity: antibodies form against the inhaled particles, antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the lung, and inflammation and granulomas follow. Alveolar walls thicken, exudate forms, and lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils fill the bronchioles; advanced cases scar.

q: what is pneumoconiosis
how does inhaled dust cause lung fibrosis
cards.x:
Occupational lung diseases come from chronic inhalation of toxic gases or inert particles such as coal, silica and asbestos. A pneumoconiosis is the specific case of lung tissue disease caused by inhaled inorganic dust.

The mechanism is a clearance failure. Toxic gases or particles disable the cilia that should sweep them out, alveolar macrophages try to engulf and remove them but fail, and the alveolar walls are damaged until the lung becomes fibrotic. Smoking and environmental pollutants contribute because they also depress ciliary function.

q: what happens in ARDS
why is the edema in ARDS noncardiogenic
why do alveoli collapse in ARDS
cards.x:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a lung injury that occurs alongside another process, such as shock, trauma, embolism, aspiration, drug overdose, radiation or disseminated intravascular coagulation. The starting event is damage to the alveolar-capillary membrane.

Three things then go wrong:
- Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema: the injured capillaries leak, flooding the alveoli with protein-rich fluid. The heart is not the cause.
- Atelectasis: without enough surfactant the alveoli collapse.
- Hyaline membranes: inflammatory deposits of protein line the air spaces.

The injury also activates complement and traps neutrophils in the lung. Because collapse is central, ARDS is classed as an atelectatic, restrictive disorder.

q: what is a pneumothorax
why does tension pneumothorax lower cardiac output
who gets a primary spontaneous pneumothorax
cards.x:
A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space, the potential space around the lung that normally holds only a little lubricating fluid.
- Primary (spontaneous): typically tall, thin men aged 20 to 40 with no lung disease; small subpleural blebs at the lung apices rupture, the lung collapses and the rib cage springs out. Smoking raises the risk.
- Secondary: a complication of existing lung disease such as asthma, emphysema, cystic fibrosis, pneumonia or tuberculosis.
- Tension: usually traumatic. Air gets in but cannot get out during expiration, acting like a one-way valve, so pressure keeps building. The lung on that side collapses and the mediastinum is pushed to the other side, which reduces venous return and cardiac output.

q: what causes a pleural effusion
what is a chylothorax
how much fluid is normally in the pleural space
cards.x:
A pleural effusion is not a disease in itself but a collection of fluid or pus in the pleural cavity caused by another process. Normally there is only 5 to 15 mL of serous fluid, made by the parietal pleural capillaries and drained by the parietal lymphatics.

Fluid builds up when the Starling balance tips:
- Higher hydrostatic pressure in the small vessels (heart failure, portal hypertension).
- Lower plasma oncotic pressure (severe hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis).
- Lower pressure in the pleural space (lung collapse).

Two special kinds: a hemothorax is blood mixed with pleural fluid, and a chylothorax is chyle leaking from the thoracic duct, after trauma or a mediastinal cancer such as lymphoma.

q: what is the difference between a transudate and an exudate
which conditions cause an exudative effusion
what LDH ratio means exudate
cards.x:
The split tells you whether the problem is pressure or a leaky, inflamed pleura.
- Transudate: low protein (pleural-to-serum protein ratio below 0.5), low lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; pleural-to-serum ratio below 0.6), specific gravity below 1.016. Caused by higher hydrostatic or lower oncotic pressure: severe heart failure, cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, myxedema.
- Exudate: protein ratio above 0.5 or LDH ratio above 0.6. Caused by a more permeable, inflamed pleura or impaired lymphatic drainage: cancer, infection, pulmonary embolism, sarcoidosis, post-myocardial infarction syndrome, pancreatic disease.

One positive criterion is enough to call it an exudate, even if the protein ratio looks transudative.

q: what is obstructive sleep apnea
what is the difference between apnea and hypopnea
how is central apnea different from obstructive apnea
cards.x:
Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome is repeated blockage of the upper airway during sleep, with symptoms or signs of disturbed sleep. The collapsible segments of the pharynx close completely or partly. At least 5 obstructive events per hour of sleep is the minimal criterion.
- Obstructive apnea: no airflow for at least 10 seconds while the person keeps trying to breathe.
- Hypopnea: airflow drops (without stopping) for at least 10 seconds, with a fall in oxygen saturation or an abrupt arousal.
- Central event: no airflow and no effort either.

Each obstruction combines building asphyxia (too little oxygen, too much carbon dioxide) with a sudden autonomic and behavioral arousal, which strains the heart and brain circulation.

q: how does pneumonia develop
what is the difference between community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia
what does gross aspiration cause
cards.x:
Pneumonia is inflammation of the alveoli and interstitium caused by an infectious agent. Organisms reach the lung three ways: aspiration of mouth and throat secretions or stomach contents (gross aspiration delivers large numbers of anaerobic bacteria and is a major factor in anaerobic infection and abscess), inhalation (viruses, Mycoplasma), or through the bloodstream (staphylococcal sepsis, right-sided endocarditis, intravenous drug use).

Normal defenses such as immune responses, cough, sneezing and mucociliary clearance keep the lungs clean; community-acquired pneumonia happens when they are compromised. The organisms multiply, the air spaces fill with exudate and it consolidates, becoming hard to cough up.

Community-acquired means living independently, or hospitalized for under 48 hours before symptoms. Hospital-acquired infections in the first 4 days tend to be antibiotic-susceptible; late-onset ones are more often multidrug-resistant.

q: what is asthma
what is the difference between allergic and non-allergic asthma
what mediates allergic asthma
cards.x:
Asthma is the obstructive airway disease whose obstruction is reversible, with airway inflammation and airways that overreact to many stimuli. Reversible is a relative word, though: long-standing inflammation and remodeling can leave some limitation that does not fully reverse.

Allergic (extrinsic) asthma is driven by immunoglobulin E: IgE on mast cells meets its antigen and the mast cells release histamine, leukotrienes (the slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis), prostaglandins, bradykinins, eosinophilic chemotactic factor and serotonin.

Non-allergic (intrinsic) asthma follows exercise, stress or irritants, with no specific allergen; drugs such as aspirin and occupational allergens are implicated. Skin tests are negative, serum IgE is normal, it often starts in middle age, and the prognosis is less favorable.

cards.t: What happens to the airway in asthma
q: what changes happen in the asthmatic airway
why can asthma testing be normal between attacks
cards.x:
In asthma the normal airway lining is stripped away (denuded) and replaced by goblet cells, which make mucus. Leaky small vessels cause mucosal swelling and inflammatory exudate, the airway muscle constricts, and arriving white cells release more mediators that damage the lining further. Vagal nerve stimulation adds mucus hypersecretion and more bronchoconstriction. Under the microscope there is collagen laid down beneath the basement membrane, edema, mast cell activation and neutrophils, eosinophils and lymphocytes. The result is bronchospasm, mucus plugs and, over time, remodeling of the airway wall.

Symptoms come and go, so testing can be normal between episodes. Muscle contraction and inflammation also recover at different speeds, so feeling better early can leave inflammation behind.

q: what causes pulmonary edema
what is noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
cards.x:
Pulmonary edema is fluid that has left the capillaries and collected in the lung. It follows the Starling forces: fluid leaves a capillary when the hydrostatic push exceeds the osmotic pull, so a rise in capillary hydrostatic pressure or a fall in plasma oncotic pressure increases filtration.

It can also come from leaky capillaries. In acute respiratory distress syndrome the injured alveolar-capillary membrane floods the alveoli with protein-rich fluid, a noncardiogenic edema, and in acute lung injury the leaked water, cells and protein collapse large areas of alveoli. Pulmonary edema is one of the lung-tissue causes of acute respiratory failure.

cards.t: Pulmonary embolism and its effects on the lung
q: how does a pulmonary embolism affect breathing
how does pulmonary embolism cause pulmonary hypertension
cards.x:
A pulmonary embolism blocks part of the pulmonary arterial tree, and its effects ripple through several topics:
- Dead space: the blocked area is still ventilated but no longer perfused, so breathing there is wasted, which pushes toward hypercapnic ventilatory failure.
- Acute respiratory failure: it is one of the lung-tissue causes.
- Pulmonary hypertension: obstruction raises resistance to blood flow.
- Acute respiratory distress syndrome: embolism is among its causes.
- Pleural effusion: it is associated with an exudate.

k: right heart failure from lung disease
q: what is cor pulmonale
how does lung disease cause right heart failure
cards.x:
Cor pulmonale is dilation of the right ventricle caused by lung disease. The chain, classically from chronic bronchitis: low oxygen makes the pulmonary arteries constrict (hypoxic vasoconstriction), the constriction causes pulmonary hypertension, the right ventricle has to pump against that pressure and dilates, and right-sided heart failure follows. The edema of that right-sided failure, plus cyanosis, is the "blue bloater" picture. Advanced emphysema can reach pulmonary hypertension by the same hypoxic route.

Pulmonary embolism also raises pulmonary pressure, but by a different route: physical obstruction rather than vasoconstriction.
